title: Google Cloud Global Service Control / IAM Outage — June 12, 2025
dcName: Google Cloud — Service Control quota system (global control plane)

severity.usersAffected: Global — customers of dozens of Google Cloud products (~70+, approximate) across every region, plus downstream end-users of dependent platforms (Cloudflare, and widely reported others such as Spotify and Discord). No authoritative aggregate end-user count published; Downdetector peak report counts (e.g. Spotify ~46k) are report tallies, not user counts.
severity.impactUsd: Not publicly quantified — no official SLA-credit total, insurer, or analyst dollar estimate located.
servicesDown: Identity and Access Management (IAM token issuance)
Vertex AI (Gemini API) / Vertex AI Search

brief: A latent, unguarded code path in Google Cloud's Service Control quota system — added on 2025-05-29 without error handling or feature-flag protection — was triggered on 2025-06-12 when a policy change containing unintended blank fields was inserted into the regional Spanner tables Service Control reads for policy data. The blank metadata replicated globally within seconds; regional quota checks pulled the blank fields, exercised the unprotected path, dereferenced a null pointer, and, with no error handling to contain it, the Service Control binaries crashed and entered a global crash loop. Because Service Control gates API authorization, IAM could no longer issue tokens and most Google Cloud APIs failed worldwide for several hours. The failure cascaded into downstream platforms that depend on GCP, most notably Cloudflare, whose Workers KV backend relied on the affected infrastructure.

magnitude.note: Global blast radius across all regions and ~70+ products (approximate) with IAM token issuance down (blast/users = 10). Duration ~7h27m end-to-end, meaningful but bounded and recoverable (7). Financial magnitude inferred high from breadth and multi-platform cascade, but no official dollar figure is published (8, low-confidence).

sequenceOfEvents.event: A new feature is added to Service Control for additional quota policy checks. The change ships with no appropriate error handling and is not feature-flag protected, leaving a latent, unguarded code path in the global quota system.
A policy change containing unintended blank fields is inserted into the regional Spanner tables that Service Control uses for policies. The metadata replicates globally within seconds.

Incident officially begins. Service Control's regional quota checks read the blank fields, exercise the unprotected May-29 code path, hit a null pointer, and — lacking error handling — the binaries crash and enter a global crash loop, so IAM can no longer issue tokens and most Google Cloud APIs fail worldwide.

Downstream Cloudflare outage begins, roughly one minute after the GCP incident starts: Cloudflare's Workers KV backend depended on the affected third-party (Google Cloud) infrastructure, degrading dependent Cloudflare products.
The 'red-button' rollout that disables the offending path is completed within 40 minutes of the incident, and recovery begins across regions, smaller regions first.

Cloudflare's outage ends. Cloudflare states the outage 'lasted 2 hours and 28 minutes'; note the stated window (17:52-20:28 UTC) spans ~2h36m by the clock, so 2h28m is Cloudflare's stated figure rather than the window arithmetic.

us-central1 takes up to ~2h40m to fully resolve — the longest region — because Google throttled Service Control task creation to minimize impact on the underlying infrastructure and routed traffic to multi-regional databases to shed load. (Wall-clock ~13:31 PDT is arithmetic, not a verbatim published timestamp.)
Incident ends ('All the services are fully recovered from the service issue'). Total end-to-end duration ~7h27m from the 10:51 PDT begin.

Status-page update stream continues past recovery with posts timestamped 23:34 PDT (12 June) and 16:45 PDT (13 June), consistent with post-incident report publication/edits rather than new customer impact.

rootCause:
On May 29, 2025, Google added a new feature to Service Control — the global control-plane component that performs per-request API management, including authorization and quota policy checks, for Google Cloud and Google Workspace products — to perform additional quota policy checks. Per Google's incident report, this change "did not have appropriate error handling nor was it feature flag protected." Because it was not feature-flag protected, it was NOT disabled by default and went live in the serving path immediately; because it lacked error handling, the new branch could not tolerate malformed policy input. The defect remained latent until data exercised the vulnerable branch roughly two weeks later.

The trigger occurred on June 12, 2025 (incident start ~10:51 PDT per the status page; a policy change was inserted shortly before). A policy change was inserted into the regional Spanner tables that Service Control uses for policies, and "this policy data contained unintended blank fields." Because quota management is global, the metadata was not rolled out gradually or region-by-region; the report states "this metadata was replicated globally within seconds," so every regional Service Control datastore received the defective policy data almost simultaneously.

The failure mechanism was deterministic and input-driven. When Service Control "regionally exercised quota checks on policies in each regional datastore," the new code path "pulled in blank fields for this respective policy change and exercised the code path that hit the null pointer causing the binaries to go into a crash loop." Lacking error handling, the null pointer was not caught as a recoverable per-request error — it crashed the process, and each restart re-read the same poisoned policy, sustaining the crash loop. Because the poisoned metadata reached every region within seconds, Service Control binaries crash-looped near-simultaneously across all regions, producing a global blast radius. With Service Control down, Google Cloud, Google Workspace and Google Security Operations products "experienced increased 503 errors in external API requests" (also described as elevated 5xx errors) worldwide.

Safeguards that could have contained the failure were absent. There was no fail-open behavior: a crash in the quota-check path took down the entire serving path rather than letting requests proceed without the check — hence Google's committed remediation to "modularize Service Control's architecture, so the functionality is isolated and fails open." Feature-flag protection that would have kept the path off by default and allowed surgical disablement was absent. Global near-instant replication of quota metadata provided no staged-rollout containment boundary. And the recovery path lacked resilience: "Service Control did not have the appropriate randomized exponential backoff implemented," so when tasks restarted after the fix they "created a herd effect on the underlying infrastructure it depends on (i.e. that Spanner table), overloading the infrastructure."

Detection was fast but recovery was slowed by that herd effect. "Within 2 minutes" SRE was triaging; "within 10 minutes, the root cause was identified and the red-button (to disable the serving path) was being put in place." The red-button was ready ~25 minutes in, and "within 40 minutes of the incident, the red-button rollout was completed, and we started seeing recovery across regions." Larger regions took materially longer: in us-central-1 the restart herd overloaded the Spanner infrastructure, and it "took up to ~2h 40 mins to fully resolve." The overall incident ended 18:18 PDT.
contributingFactors: Missing error handling in the new quota-policy-check code path: the branch added May 29, 2025 could not tolerate malformed input, so a blank policy field produced an unhandled null pointer that crashed the binary instead of being caught ('did not have appropriate error handling').

Absence of feature-flag protection on a critical binary change: because the new code path 'was not feature flag protected' it was not disabled by default and went straight into the live serving path, and could not be surgically disabled — forcing a full 'red-button' serving-path shutdown.

No fail-open isolation in Service Control's architecture: a fault in one quota-check function brought down the entire serving path globally rather than degrading gracefully, which Google is remediating by modularizing the architecture 'so the functionality is isolated and fails open.'

Global, near-instant replication of quota metadata: the design that replicated policy data 'globally within seconds' provided no staged-rollout containment boundary, so a single defective policy change poisoned every regional datastore almost simultaneously.

Lack of randomized exponential backoff in restart/retry logic: when tasks restarted after mitigation they stampeded the Spanner tables, 'creating a herd effect on the underlying infrastructure ... overloading the infrastructure,' materially prolonging recovery in large regions such as us-central-1 (~2h40m).

Insufficient validation of replicated policy data: the 'unintended blank fields' propagated into the serving path without validation that would have caught the malformed data, consistent with Google's commitment to audit global data-replication and metadata-propagation systems.

coe.action: Modularize Service Control so it fails open — serving degraded results rather than crashing — when it encounters invalid or blank metadata.
Enforce that all changes to critical binaries are feature-flag protected and rolled out incrementally rather than activated globally and instantly.
Improve static analysis and testing practices to catch this class of defect (unhandled null/exception on a critical path) before it ships.
Audit all systems that consume globally-replicated data for equivalent unvalidated-input exposure, and ensure such data is propagated/consumed safely.
Audit and ensure Service Control uses randomized exponential backoff on task restart/retry to prevent the herd effect that overloaded infrastructure during recovery.
Ensure monitoring and external customer-communication infrastructure remains operational even when Google Cloud itself is down, so customers get information as soon as possible.

lessonsLearnt: Critical control-plane code must fail open, not crash — a null dereference on invalid input should degrade service, never take down a global authorization path.

Every change to a globally-replicated, blast-radius-wide system must ship behind a feature flag with incremental rollout; instant global activation removes the only chance to catch a bad change in staging before it is everywhere.

Systems that consume globally-replicated metadata must validate that data at the point of use; a single blank-field insert replicating in seconds is enough to weaponize an unvalidated read path across every region.

Recovery of a large control plane is itself a distributed-systems problem — mass task restarts create a herd effect, so recovery needs randomized exponential backoff, throttled task creation, and load re-routing, which realistically lengthens time-to-restore in the biggest regions.

Concentrating authorization in one shared component (Service Control/IAM) makes it a single point of failure whose blast radius spans ~70+ products and cascades to external customers who depend on GCP.
Monitoring and customer-communication tooling must not share fate with the platform they observe; when Google Cloud went down, the ability to monitor and communicate must survive independently.
improvements: Introduce fail-open modularization in Service Control so invalid metadata yields degraded-but-available authorization instead of a crash loop.
Mandate feature-flagged, incremental rollout for all changes to global control-plane systems, replacing instant global activation.
Add error handling and static-analysis/testing coverage across critical binary code paths to catch unhandled null/exception conditions pre-release.
Systematically audit and harden all consumers of globally-replicated data against blank/malformed inputs.
Stand up monitoring and external-communication infrastructure that remains operational independently of Google Cloud's own health.

Adopt throttled, load-aware recovery procedures — randomized exponential backoff, task-creation throttling, and multi-regional database routing — as a standard playbook to avoid herd-effect overload during control-plane restarts.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Failure mechanism
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The outage was a textbook latent-defect-meets-bad-data failure. On 2025-05-29 a quota-policy-check feature entered Service Control without error handling or a feature flag, creating a dormant, unguarded code path. It stayed inert until 2025-06-12, when a policy insert with unintended blank fields landed in the regional Spanner policy tables. When quota checks read those blank fields, they exercised the unguarded path and dereferenced a null pointer. With nothing to catch the fault, the binaries did not degrade — they crashed, and immediately restarted into the same poisoned state, producing a self-sustaining crash loop.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Why it cascaded
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Two amplifiers turned a local defect into a global outage. First, the triggering metadata replicated to every region within seconds, so there was no staggered exposure and effectively no detect-and-halt window — every region hit the null pointer at nearly the same moment. Second, Service Control sits on the authorization critical path: when it crash-looped, IAM could not issue tokens, and without tokens most Google Cloud APIs across ~70+ products failed simultaneously. The blast radius then extended beyond Google: platforms built on GCP failed downstream, most notably Cloudflare, whose Workers KV backend depended on the affected infrastructure, dragging down Durable Objects/D1, AI Gateway, Pages, Stream, Realtime and Images for roughly a 2.5-hour window (17:52–20:28 UTC; Cloudflare states the outage lasted 2h28m).

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Detection, mitigation and recovery
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Mitigation was fast; full recovery was deliberately slow. Engineers identified the offending path and completed a 'red-button' rollout within ~40 minutes of the 10:51 PDT begin, after which regions recovered smaller-first. But bringing Service Control back was itself a distributed-systems hazard: restarting all tasks at once risked a herd-effect overload of the underlying infrastructure. Google therefore throttled Service Control task creation and routed traffic to multi-regional databases to shed load, which is why us-central1 — the largest region — took up to ~2h40m to fully resolve (implying ~13:31 PDT, an arithmetic estimate). The incident was declared over at 18:18 PDT, ~7h27m end-to-end, with status-page posts continuing to 23:34 PDT (12 Jun) and 16:45 PDT (13 Jun) as post-incident publication rather than new impact.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Organizational and systemic factors
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The corrective actions read as an admission that process guardrails, not just code, failed. A change reached a global, blast-radius-wide system with neither error handling nor a feature flag, and a consumer of globally-replicated data trusted that data without validating it. The remediation set — fail-open modularization, mandatory incremental feature-flagged rollout, static analysis on critical paths, an audit of all global-metadata consumers, randomized exponential backoff to blunt the recovery herd effect, and independent monitoring/communication infrastructure — targets each systemic gap. The last item is notable: it concedes that observability and customer comms shared fate with the platform, so operators were partly blind and constrained in communicating precisely when they most needed both.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Cross-incident pattern
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: This incident fits a recurring cloud-era failure archetype: a single shared control-plane component (identity/authorization/quota) becomes a global single point of failure, and a benign-looking configuration or metadata change — not a hardware fault — triggers correlated, simultaneous failure everywhere at once. The same shape recurs across major providers: unvalidated input or a bad config replicates faster than humans can react, an unhandled exception converts a data problem into a crash, and deep dependency graphs turn one vendor's control-plane outage into a multi-company internet event. The durable lesson across all of them is identical to Google's own action items: validate replicated inputs, fail open on the critical path, and roll changes out incrementally with flags.

technicalDeepDive:
Service Control is Google's control-plane component responsible for per-request API management — including authorization and quota enforcement — for Google Cloud and Google Workspace APIs. It reads policy configuration from regional Spanner tables and, per request, exercises quota checks against the policies in that region's datastore. On May 29, 2025 an additional quota-policy-check code path was added to this hot serving path. Two safeguards were missing on that change: the report states it "did not have appropriate error handling nor was it feature flag protected." The absence of the flag meant the code was active in production and not disabled by default; the absence of error handling meant the branch assumed well-formed policy data.

The latent defect was activated by data, not by a subsequent code deploy. On June 12 a policy change carrying "unintended blank fields" was written into the regional Spanner policy tables. When Service Control "regionally exercised quota checks on policies in each regional datastore," the new code path "pulled in blank fields for this respective policy change and exercised the code path that hit the null pointer causing the binaries to go into a crash loop." Because there was no surrounding error handling, this was not a recoverable per-request error; on restart the same poisoned policy was re-read and re-evaluated, sustaining the crash loop.

The blast radius was global and near-simultaneous because of the replication topology. Quota management is globally consistent, so "this metadata was replicated globally within seconds," and each regional Service Control instance independently exercised the same fatal check against its local datastore. There was no gradual or canaried rollout of this data to act as a circuit breaker, so regions entered the crash loop at essentially the same time, and dependent APIs across Google Cloud, Workspace and Security Operations returned increased 503 / 5xx errors worldwide.

Recovery dynamics were dominated by a thundering-herd problem. The mitigation was a "red-button (to disable the serving path)," identified within 10 minutes, ready ~25 minutes in, and rolled out within 40 minutes, at which point recovery began across regions. But when Service Control tasks restarted en masse they hammered the Spanner tables they depend on. Because "Service Control did not have the appropriate randomized exponential backoff implemented," the synchronized retry storm "created a herd effect on the underlying infrastructure ... overloading the infrastructure" — most acutely in large regions such as us-central-1, which required throttling and rerouting and "took up to ~2h 40 mins to fully resolve," even though the serving-path fix rolled out within ~40 minutes. The incident ended at 18:18 PDT.

sourcing.confidence: high — root cause, timeline (10:51 PDT begin, +40min red button, ~2h40m us-central1, 18:18 PDT end / 7h27m), recovery method and remediation verbatim-verified from the primary Google Cloud incident report; Cloudflare cascade metrics verified from Cloudflare's own postmortem.
